summary:
CLPS Mission Planner is an interactive web app (built with Python and Streamlit) that helps teams pick and assess landing sites for commercial robotic missions at the lunar south pole. It uses JPL Horizons ephemerides together with terrain data from NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap, and runs five linked models: (1) solar illumination, (2) Earth visibility for direct-to-Earth communication, (3) terrain and landing safety, (4) solar power generation, and (5) power consumption and battery survival. An interactive 3D terrain viewer lets users compare 4 baseline sites and 12 research candidates side by side.

The challenge asks how the Sun and Earth move across the lunar sky. Our tool answers that and carries it through to whether a mission is viable: terrain shapes the horizon, the horizon controls sunlight and Earth contact, and those decide whether a lander can make enough power to survive. At the south pole, low sun angles and long shadows make site choice the difference between mission success and failure. As Artemis and CLPS traffic grows, our open, data-driven tool helps smaller teams, students and new commercial providers do credible early mission planning.
details:
Live demo: https://lunarsouthteam.streamlit.app/

CLPS Mission Planner is a decision-support web app for planning commercial robotic landings (NASA CLPS-class missions) at the lunar south pole. A user picks a candidate landing site and a mission window. The app then runs five linked models and shows where a lander would get sunlight, talk to Earth, land safely, and survive the night.

HOW IT WORKS – FIVE MODELS

1. Illumination: computes the Sun's position at each site (JPL Horizons) against the local terrain horizon, giving the percentage of time the site is sunlit.

2. Earth Visibility / Direct-to-Earth Communication: finds the windows when Earth is above the local horizon, so the lander can talk to Earth directly without a relay.

3. Terrain & Landing Safety: uses elevation and slope data from NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap to flag steep slopes, roughness and hazards.

4. Power Generation: turns illumination into expected solar-array output over the mission timeline, accounting for low sun angles at the pole.

5. Power Consumption & Battery Survival: models subsystem loads against generation and battery state of charge, predicting whether the lander survives dark periods and how long it can operate.

An interactive 3D terrain viewer brings the results together. Users can explore each site and compare 4 baseline sites against 12 research candidates side by side.

BENEFITS

- Combines illumination, communication, terrain and power into one workflow. These analyses are usually done separately.

- Gives a quick first-pass look at site viability, so teams can rule sites in or out early.

- Visual and interactive, so non-specialists can see why one site is better than another.

INTENDED IMPACT

As Artemis and CLPS missions increase traffic to the lunar south pole, site selection decides whether a mission works. We want to lower the barrier for students, universities and new commercial providers to do credible early mission planning with openly available NASA data.

TOOLS & TECHNOLOGIES

- Language: Python

- Framework: Streamlit (web app and deployment)

- Libraries: NumPy and others for numerical modelling; 3D plotting for the terrain viewer

- Data: JPL Horizons, NASA Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap (NASA LRO data), Canadian Space Agency Moon Exploration resources

- Development: Claude Code (AI coding assistant) for code generation, refactoring and debugging

- Hardware: A standard laptop running Kali Linux. No special hardware is needed, and the app runs in any web browser.

CREATIVITY

Most site-selection tools look at one factor at a time. Ours links them as a chain: terrain shapes the horizon, the horizon controls sunlight and Earth visibility, sunlight drives power, and power decides survival. Users can see why a site fails, not just that it fails. The 3D viewer turns abstract numbers into terrain users can explore.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Extremely low sun angles and long shadows at the south pole

- Earth line-of-sight for direct communication

- Slope and hazard limits for safe touchdown

- Battery sizing and survival through dark periods

- Open, publicly available data, so anyone can reproduce the results

- An interface that non-experts can use

SI DISCLOSURE

Parts of the code and text were developed with Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI assistant. The team directed and reviewed all models, data choices and outputs. No NASA branding was generated or modified.
